input:
Reaction kinetics is a cornerstone of chemical engineering, and the temperature dependence of reaction rates is one of the most important aspects of the subject. This passage reports measurements of the rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction at two temperatures. Measurements at each temperature were carried out in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was found to be 4%, indicating good reproducibility. The reaction was studied in the liquid phase, and the measurements were performed in a manner designed to ensure that the samples analysed were representative of the reacting mixture at each of the temperatures investigated.

At 300 K, the rate constant was measured as k = 0.029 s-1. At 340 K, the value of k was 2.331 s-1. It should be noted that this value is a derived value rather than a directly measured one, having been computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 93 kJ mol-1.

The increase in temperature of 40 K therefore corresponds to an increase in the rate constant from 0.029 s-1 to 2.331 s-1, demonstrating the strong sensitivity of the reaction rate to temperature. This behaviour is consistent with the well-known exponential dependence embodied in the Arrhenius relation.

Unfortunately, no rate constant is reported above 340 K. This is because, above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, which made it impossible to obtain reliable samples under those conditions. Further work would be needed to extend the measurements beyond this limit, perhaps by adopting a modified sampling technique, highlighting the practical challenges that can arise in experimental kinetics and the care needed when interpreting values that have been derived rather than measured directly.
target:
The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. A first-order reaction has a rate proportional to the concentration of the single reactant it consumes, and k is the constant of that proportionality: the larger k, the larger the fraction of reactant consumed in each second at a given concentration. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. The measurements were made on the reacting liquid itself, at the temperature of the reaction, and the constant reported for each temperature is the value the triplicate measurements returned.

At 300 K, k = 0.029 s-1. At 340 K, k = 2.331 s-1. The second value is derived, not measured: it is computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 93 kJ mol-1, and it is stated as a derived value wherever it is used.

The interval between the temperatures is 40 K, and across it the constant rises from the measured 0.029 s-1 to the derived 2.331 s-1. The pair of values is therefore a statement about temperature sensitivity anchored at its measured end. The derived end carries the scatter of the measurements and, in addition, whatever error the activation energy holds; the standard deviation quoted belongs to the measurements and does not extend to the derivation.

No rate constant is reported above 340 K. Above that temperature the solvent evaporated during sampling, and a sample that loses solvent while it is collected no longer carries the composition of the reacting liquid. The limit sits in the sampling step, not in the reaction: the reported range ends at 340 K because measurement failed there, not because the kinetics changed. The same point governs any use of the pair outside the interval: an extrapolation carries the derivation further from its measured anchor, and the sampling limit that closed the range stands in the way of checking it.
